I am a rather elderly man, a lawyer who has spent thirty years in a snug business among rich mens bonds, mortgages, and title deeds, and of all the strange scriveners I have known, Bartleby was the strangest. <break time="0.8s" /> Of his life before he came to me nothing can be known, for, except what my own astonished eyes saw of him, there exist no materials for a full biography of the man. <break time="0.8s" /> My office stood up one flight of stairs on Wall Street, and its windows commanded, at one end, a white wall inside a light shaft and, at the other, a lofty brick wall black with age. <break time="0.8s" /> Turkey, an Englishman of about sixty, was a most valuable copyist before noon, but after his midday meal his face blazed like a coal fire, and he blotted his papers with reckless haste. <break time="0.8s" /> Nippers, a young man of five and twenty, suffered from ambition and indigestion in the mornings, when he ground his teeth over his desk, yet in the afternoons he was comparatively mild. <break time="0.8s" /> Since their fits came on in turn, like guards relieving one another, I never had to deal with both eccentricities at once, and a twelve year old boy, nicknamed Ginger Nut, ran our errands for cakes and apples. <break time="0.8s" /> When business increased, I advertised for another copyist, and one summer morning there stood upon my office threshold a motionless young man, pallidly neat, pitiably respectable, incurably forlorn. <break time="0.8s" /> Thinking that his sedate manner might have a good effect upon the flighty Turkey and the fiery Nippers, I placed his desk behind a high green folding screen, close to a small window that looked upon a wall.

At first Bartleby did an extraordinary quantity of writing, as if long famishing for something to copy, but he worked on silently, palely, and mechanically, without a trace of cheerful industry. <break time="0.8s" /> On the third day, when I called him to examine a short paper with me, he replied, in a singularly mild, firm voice, I would prefer not to. <break time="0.8s" /> Had there been the least uneasiness, anger, or impertinence in his manner, I would have dismissed him at once, but his face was leanly composed and his gray eye dimly calm. <break time="0.8s" /> A few days later, when the four copies of a long document were ready to be examined, I called all my clerks together, but Bartleby, appearing at the entrance of his hermitage, calmly preferred not to join us. <break time="0.8s" /> When I demanded his reasons, he merely repeated, I would prefer not to, and, as often happens to a man resisted in some unprecedented way, I began to stagger in my own plainest faith. <break time="0.8s" /> Turning to my other clerks for support, I asked their opinion, whereupon Turkey declared, in his mild morning voice, that I was quite right, and Nippers proposed to kick the scrivener out of the office. <break time="0.8s" /> Nothing so aggravates an earnest person as passive resistance, yet, because Bartleby seemed to mean no harm, I resolved to construe his strange conduct charitably rather than to punish it. <break time="0.8s" /> To befriend him, I reasoned, would cost me little or nothing, while it would lay up in my soul what would eventually prove a sweet morsel for my conscience.
